tagline: The Costa Verde and beyond — a green coast of islands an hour from a megacity.
summary: Brazil's southeastern seaboard packs a rare combination: Rio de Janeiro, a coastal megacity of millions, sits an hour's water from the Costa Verde — Angra dos Reis, Ilha Grande and a labyrinth of 365 islands — while Florianópolis anchors a second island-and-marina cluster to the south. Today the leisure and commuter flows across this water run on slow ferries, schooner day-trips and private launches. A clean, fast, stabilised foiling tier is the premium-but-practical layer Brazil's coast has never had.
why_marine_mobility: Brazil's coastal story is not one city — it is the corridor between Rio and the Costa Verde and the marina belt around Florianópolis. From Rio's marinas to Angra dos Reis and Ilha Grande is a short, scenic, congested-on-land run that is far better made on the water; today it is a slow ferry or a private boat. Navier's Pioneer II foiling tier turns those crossings into smooth, dry, on-demand legs, while the same craft serves the dense marina-to-marina hops around both Angra/Costa Verde and Florianópolis — leisure and coastal commute on one clean platform.

demand_signals.label: Costa Verde leisure density
demand_signals.note: Angra dos Reis and Ilha Grande — a 365-island archipelago of beaches, marinas and resorts — draw heavy yacht, charter and day-trip traffic from Rio's affluent market.

demand_signals.label: Rio megacity adjacency
demand_signals.note: A metropolitan population of millions sits within Pioneer II range of the Costa Verde, where road access is slow and winding — a natural coastal-commute and weekend-flow corridor.

demand_signals.label: Florianópolis marina belt
demand_signals.note: Florianópolis and Santa Catarina concentrate a dense cluster of marinas and island beaches with established boating culture and high domestic-tourism volume.

use_cases.body: Rio (Costa Verde marinas) to Angra dos Reis and Ilha Grande: the flagship leisure corridor, flown smooth and dry on Pioneer II in place of a slow ferry or schooner — a premium day-island and resort transfer.
Costa Verde marina-to-marina hops: short Bracuhy–Cacolaco-type legs around Angra served on demand, turning a fragmented marina belt into a connected clean shuttle network.
Florianópolis marina shuttles: clean, quiet Pioneer II hops between the island's marinas and beach clubs, matching a high-end domestic leisure market with no comparable water product today.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The entire cluster sits inside Pioneer II's 70-nautical-mile range: the Rio–Angra/Ilha Grande Costa Verde corridor (≈8–14 nm of open run), the dense Angra marina hops, and the Florianópolis marina belt are all commercial-ready today at 30 knots.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Longer coastal trunks — linking the Rio/Costa Verde cluster southward toward Florianópolis (~300+ nm) or up the seaboard — are Quanta-LR corridors (~700 nm hybrid range, H2 2026+), opening line-haul legs no day-boat can serve.

signature_routes.label: Rio de Janeiro (Costa Verde) ↔ Angra dos Reis / Ilha Grande — the headline leisure corridor
Costa Verde marina hop — Marina Bracuhy ↔ Marina Cacolaco (Angra)

transit_planning: For a marina group, resort operator or regional tourism authority: a clean, fast, on-demand water tier that connects Rio's affluent market to the Costa Verde and stitches together the fragmented Angra and Florianópolis marina belts. Start with the proven short Costa Verde and Florianópolis hops on Pioneer II — riding existing berths and jetties with no new infrastructure — then extend to longer coastal trunks on Quanta-LR as range comes online.
competitive_landscape: Coastal travel here runs on conventional ferries (cheap but slow and fixed-schedule), schooner day-trips (scenic but unhurried) and private launches (fast but diesel and costly to run). There is no clean, on-demand premium tier. Navier's foiling craft is the missing option: faster and smoother than a ferry, cleaner and quieter than a diesel launch, and matched to an affluent leisure market that has no comparable water product today.
regulatory_note: Brazilian maritime passenger transport is overseen by the Marinha do Brasil (Brazilian Navy) port-captaincy system and ANTAQ (the national waterway transport agency); passenger operation requires vessel registration and crew certification under the Tribunal Marítimo framework. State and municipal tourism authorities in Rio de Janeiro and Santa Catarina are natural first touchpoints.
seasonality: The Brazilian summer (Dec–Mar) brings peak leisure demand and the calmest, warmest conditions across the Costa Verde and Florianópolis; the southern winter (Jun–Aug) is cooler with more frontal weather pushing up from the south — the shoulder window where a stabilised foiling craft holds comfort and schedule when conventional craft get rough.

precedents.what: Four Seasons Lake Austin operates an N30 in live luxury-hospitality service — proof of the premium water-shuttle model Navier brings to Brazil's coastal and island corridors.
